messages.author: 5b427c05fb1416e3
messages.subject: memory and scantwo
parts:
Hi everyone:

I'm running the most recent version of Rqtl on a recombinant inbred
mapping population using a workstation wtih 2 gigs RAM and two
processors.
I'm running into an error message when I run permutations in scantwo.

Doing permutation in batch mode........
error cannot allocate vector of size 314064kb
in addition: warning message
1. reached total allocation of 1024mb: see help (memory.size)
2. reached total allocation of 1024mb: see help(memory.size)

I don't think I've ever had this statement when running permutations
before - maybe something to do with "batch mode"?

Can I change the max memory allocated to "R"?
I've tried this using '--max-mem-size'....but am still running into the
error.
Love to hear any thoughts.
Tom

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: memory and scantwo
parts:
You're running out of memory. help(Memory) and help("Memory-limits")
give
further information. Try doing a smaller number of permutations at a
time.

karl

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: memory and scantwo
parts:
I understand now...the reason for the memory problem is that
with methods "hk" and "imp", scanone and scantwo now do permutations
in "batch mode". A batch of permuted phenotypes is created,
and these are analyzed simultaneously using multivariate linear
regression. With a really large number of individuals, this could
be a memory hog.

I guess we need to add an argument that prevents this from happening...
force the usual approach which would use require less memory but more
computation.

In the meantime, the results of the scantwo permutations is a matrix
with two columns. You can concatenate those together using rbind().

Also, the permutations with scanone and scantwo are not terribly
complicated, so you could just do things from scratch with something
like the following:

temp <- mycross
n.perm <- 1000
for(i in 1:n.perm) {
temp$pheno <- temp$pheno[sample(nind(temp)),]
output <- scantwo(temp, ....)
[save the interesting bits from the output]
}

karl
